case_studies.title: MOSS: Self-Evolution through Source-Level Rewriting in Autonomous Agent Systems
case_studies.abstract: Autonomous agentic systems are largely static after deployment: they do not learn from user interactions, and recurring failures persist until the next human-driven update ships a fix. Self-evolving agents have emerged in response, but all confine evolution to text-mutable artifacts -- skill files, prompt configurations, memory schemas, workflow graphs -- and leave the agent harness untouched. Since routing, hook ordering, state invariants, and dispatch live in code rather than in any text artifact, an entire class of structural failure is physically unreachable from the text layer. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of autonomous agent systems being static after deployment by building a system called MOSS that enables self-evolution through source-level rewriting. The result is a system that can learn from user interactions and adapt to changes without human intervention. This research focuses on autonomous agent systems and may not be directly relevant to cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on autonomous agent systems and their internal evolution, rather than cloud infrastructure management or operations.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty: The concept of self-evolving autonomous agents is new, but the abstract lacks concrete IT relevance. Relevance: The paper touches on autonomous agent systems which is relevant to agentic systems but is not directly applicable to current IT infrastructure. Value: Potential to improve agent architecture, though specific use cases and automation opportunities are unclear. Therefore: 5 novelty points for the abstract and related research. 20 for relevance in agentic systems.  30 for value, as it's somewhat unclear but with potential for improvement.

case_studies.title: Skill Weaving: Efficient LLM Improvement via Modular Skillpacks
case_studies.abstract: Large language models increasingly require specialization across diverse domains, yet existing approaches struggle to balance multi-domain capacities with strict memory and inference constraints. In this work, we introduce SkillWeave, a modular improvement framework that enables LLMs to specialize under fixed memory budgets. SkillWeave partitions full capabilities of a general-purpose model into skillpacks -- lightweight, domain-specific delta modules -- that reorganize and refine the model's internal knowledge. SkillWeave enables large language models to specialize in diverse domains under fixed memory budgets. This framework is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.

case_studies.title: FAME: Failure-Aware Mixture-of-Experts for Message-Level Log Anomaly Detection
case_studies.abstract: Production systems generate millions of log lines daily, yet most anomaly detectors operate at the session or window-level, flagging groups of lines rather than identifying the specific message responsible. This coarse granularity forces operators to inspect many routine lines per alert. Message-level detection offers finer granularity, but remains challenging. A single event template may correspond to both normal and anomalous messages, failures arise from heterogeneous subsystems, and line-level labeling at scale is impractical. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of identifying specific log message anomalies in production systems, the team built a Failure-Aware Mixture-of-Experts system called FAME, and the result is a finer granularity in anomaly detection. FAME can identify the specific message responsible for an anomaly, rather than just flagging groups of lines. This can help reduce the workload of operators inspecting routine lines per alert.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure with large log volumes, here is what to do: review your current log anomaly detection tools, consider implementing a message-level detection system like FAME, and assess the potential benefits of reduced false positives and operator workload. This flags a risk: if your org relies on session or window-level anomaly detection, check your current alerting system for potential blind spots. Not directly applicable to all IT infrastructure work, but relevant for teams dealing with large-scale log data.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Interesting use of LLMs for log anomaly detection, but relevance is somewhat IT-centric and actionable value is moderate. Low signal since total score < 40.

case_studies.title: Governance by Construction for Generalist Agents
case_studies.abstract: Enterprise agents are increasingly expected to operate autonomously across tools and interfaces, yet production deployments require governance by construction. Systems must specify which actions are allowed, when human oversight is required, and what information may be exposed, without rebuilding the agent for each domain. This demo presents CUGA's policy system, a modular policy-as-code layer that composes with a generalist LLM agent to deliver predictable, auditable, and compliance-aware behavior in compound workflows without model fine-tuning. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of governing autonomous agents in enterprise environments, building a modular policy-as-code layer called CUGA, which results in predictable and auditable behavior. The CUGA system allows for governance by construction without requiring model fine-tuning. This enables generalist agents to operate across different tools and interfaces while ensuring compliance and security.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure with autonomous agents, here is what to do: review your current governance policies, consider implementing a policy-as-code layer like CUGA, and assess how it can be integrated with your existing agent workflows. This flags a risk: if your organisation uses generalist LLM agents, check your current governance and oversight mechanisms immediately to ensure compliance and security. Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work without autonomous agents.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper's focus on runtime governance architecture for generalist LLM agents has some relevance to IT infrastructures. However, novel aspects are primarily in AI/ML and don't break new ground in terms of existing deployments. The concept is specific and could be applied in 90 days, but requires implementation expertise.

case_studies.title: Validating Navmesh using Geometry: Voxel-Based Analysis with Prioritized Exploration
case_studies.abstract: Navigation mesh (Navmesh) inconsistencies affect the player experience by directly impacting the navigation systems used by non-playable characters (NPCs) in game environments. While navmeshes are generated from world geometry using well-established algorithms, environments change throughout development as terrain is adjusted and assets are moved or replaced, resulting in mismatches between the navmesh and the actual environment. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of navigation mesh inconsistencies in game environments by building a voxel-based analysis system with prioritized exploration, resulting in more accurate navigation systems. The system detects mismatches between the navmesh and the actual environment, improving the player experience. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.
